newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's LDP calls for coalition partners.
newsitem.headline: Japan's LDP calls for coalition partners.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party appeared to fail to win a clear majority in Japan's general election on Sunday and said it would hunt for coalition partners.

Television exit polls said the LDP, hurt by a record low turnout, could fall about 10 seats short of the 251 it needed to govern alone and end three years of coalition rule. The LDP was the senior partner in the outgoing government.

"In order to secure a comfortable majority of 270 seats in parliament we will have to form a coalition," Taku Yamasaki, head of the LDP's policy research council, told a news conference at party headquarters.
Japan's authoritative NHK public television said the LDP was heading for a tally of around 240 seats, up about 30 on its previous strength.
But it said there was a chance that the LDP might scrape home with a slim majority.
In another exit poll, Nippon Television (NTV) said Hashimoto's party would fall well short of an outright majority, with only around 237 seats.

Voter turnout was estimated at 58 percent, down almost 10 percentage points from the previous low set in the last general elections in 1993. Japan has held 19 general elections under the 1947 postwar democratic constitution, with turnout generally in the low 70 percent range.
"I'm worried about the voting turnout. We did the best we could," Hashimoto had told reporters in his first public appearance on election day.
In the outgoing parliament, the conservative LDP held 211 seats in a 511-seat Lower House and governed in a coalition with the Social Democrats and Sakigake, an LDP splinter group.
Going into the election, the two junior coalition partners had left open whether they would continue their link-up with the conservative LDP.
The smaller parties looked set to win about 20 seats between them, down from 39 in the old parliament.
Hashimoto took over as prime minister in January and called the election four weeks ago. The LDP had been in the ruling coalition since mid-1994.

The main opposition grouping Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), which held 160 seats in the outgoing parliament, was forecast to either maintain its strength or lose a few seats, with the other seats split among other liberal parties.
The polls said the fledgling Democratic Party, formed only last month with 52 Lower House defectors from the Social Democrats and Sakigake, was expected to maintain its numbers.
The only clear winner appeared to be the Japan Communist Party, which exit polls said could increase its seats to 25 from 15.

Sunday's vote for a 500-seat Lower House in a revised electoral system was the first general election since 1993, when the pro-business LDP lost its 38-year unbroken grip on power, ushering in a period of coalition rule.
Political leaders had described the election as a "landmark" and "turning point" because the four-year term for the Lower House means the new government could lead Japan into the 21st century.

The election was held nearly one year ahead of schedule because of Hashimoto's belief that he could win sole power for the LDP amid an improving economy and success in cooling down opposition to the presence of U.S. troops in Okinawa.

A record 1,503 candidates from nine parties contested the poll. The new system, in which multi-seat constituencies were abolished, was intended to foster debate on larger policy issues and root out efforts by candidates to appeal to voters with promises of lavish spending on local projects.
Voters elected 300 single-seat candidates, while 200 seats were decided by proportional representation.
In the main policy difference, Shinshinto opposed an LDP plan to raise the sales tax to five percent from three percent next April and said it would freeze the sales tax and cut income taxes.
